sections.title: Problem
sections.html:
Bangladesh throws away value it already owns.

Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter. Its factories produce a huge stream of cutting waste called jhut. The Circular Fashion Partnership (with BGMEA) measured 577,000 tonnes of post-industrial textile waste in 2019, about 250,000 tonnes of it 100% cotton. Today the figure is about 600,000 tonnes a year.

~600k tjhut per year
$235/tmixed, unsorted
$600/tsorted white cotton
~70%of sorters are women

Jhut's value depends almost entirely on sorting by fabric type and colour. Today, workers in informal yards sort it by hand and by eye. The work is slow, inconsistent and unrecorded. So most jhut is sold mixed at about $235 a tonne, while Bangladesh imports cotton fibre for its spinning mills.

sections.title: Solution
sections.html:
A phone camera that sorts jhut and records every bundle.

A worker places a scrap or bundle under a phone camera at the sorting table. Within about a second, Jhut AI:

  1. reads the colour and colour purity with pixel analysis;
  2. predicts the fabric type (jersey, denim, twill, canvas, fleece, corduroy) with a vision model;
  3. assigns a grade (A/B/C) and one of 6 bins, with a one-line Bangla instruction (for example, “বিন ১ → জার্সি · সাদা · গ্রেড A”);
  4. logs the bundle in a batch ledger, issues a Batch Passport with a QR code, and writes a daily Bangla summary for the trader.

When the AI is wrong, the worker fixes it with one tap. Every correction becomes new training data.

sections.title: Why Now
sections.html:
• The EU Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) and textile Extended Producer Responsibility push brands towards recycled, traceable content.
  • The EU ban on destroying unsold textiles applies from July 2026.
  • The coming Digital Product Passport means buyers will expect sorted, documented recycled material.
  • Phone cameras and small on-device models are now good enough to run in an informal yard, without industrial machines.

Hand sorting produces neither consistent grades nor records. Without both, Bangladesh risks losing value and buyers.

sections.title: Product Demo
sections.html:
The interactive prototype is live: Open the Jhut AI prototype →

Try it with ▶ Play auto demo. The demo scans 10 sample scraps, then fills the batch ledger, the Batch Passport and the Bangla report. The numbers in System status above update from your own demo session.

What is real in the demo: colour and grade come from pixel analysis running in the page. What is simulated: fabric predictions for the sample scraps are preset, uploaded photos use a simple texture rule (the trained model is in progress), the scale is simulated, and prices are illustrative.

sections.title: Market Opportunity
sections.html:
• Volume: about 600,000 t of jhut a year in Bangladesh; about 250,000 t of it is pure cotton.
  • Price gap: about $235/t mixed versus about $600/t for sorted white cotton, up to 2.5× for the same material.
  • National value: SWITCH2CE estimates local recycling could save Bangladesh about $700 million a year.
  • Expansion: India, Pakistan and Vietnam have the same garment-waste problem.

Figures are rounded and prices are indicative. Sources are listed at the end of this page.

sections.title: Business Model
sections.html:
• Station subscription: a monthly fee per sorting station (phone app + light box + dashboard), paid by jhut traders and factories.
  • Batch Passport fee: a small fee per verified passport issued to buyers and recyclers.
  • Later: anonymised, aggregated waste data for brands' sustainability reporting, and a commission on a marketplace that connects sorted-jhut sellers with recyclers.

Why customers pay (illustrative, to validate in pilots): a yard sorting 300 kg a day that moves part of its stock from the mixed price (about Tk 29/kg) to sorted grades (about Tk 45–73/kg) earns several thousand taka more per day. The subscription is a small fraction of that.

sections.title: Traction
sections.html:
Stage: pre-pilot. We report only what exists today.

  • Interactive prototype live, covering the full workflow (scan, ledger, passport, Bangla report).
  • Open training data identified: the Kaggle “Mobile-Captured Fabric Dataset” (3,354 phone photos taken in a textile factory, 6 classes; licence listed as unknown, so used for research and prototyping only).
  • Next: interviews and letters of interest from jhut traders, a model trained on real tailor-shop scraps, and a 4-week pilot at one sorting yard.

sections.title: Unique Advantage
sections.html:
• Sorting and traceability in one tool.
  • Phone-first and low-cost: a phone and a light box, not an industrial machine.
  • Bangla-first design for workers and traders.
  • A correction loop: every one-tap fix becomes labelled data, so the model improves with daily use.
  • Export-ready records: the Batch Passport links informal yards to EU traceability demands.

sections.title: Go-To-Market
sections.html:
1. Interviews: interview jhut traders and collect letters of interest.
  2. Free pilot: a 4-week pilot at one sorting yard, measuring price uplift and kg sorted per worker per day.
  3. Paid stations: convert pilot yards, then expand through trader networks.
  4. Demand side: offer Batch Passports to recyclers and spinning mills that need verified input.

sections.title: Vision
sections.html:
Every kilogram of garment waste sorted, recorded and recycled where it is made.

We are starting with one yard and one phone. The goal is a traceable circular supply chain for South and South-East Asia's garment hubs, where sorted waste becomes recycled fibre for local mills.

sections.title: Product Overview
sections.html:
What it does: it turns a smartphone into a sorting station that classifies textile scraps by colour and fabric, assigns a grade and bin, and records each bundle for traceability.

Target users: jhut traders and sorting yards (paying customers), garment factories, recyclers and spinning mills, and sorters, most of whom are women.

Core use cases: sort a scrap into the right bin; record a batch with weight and value; issue a Batch Passport to a buyer; send the trader a plain-Bangla daily summary.

sections.title: Data Layer
sections.html:
• Sources: the Kaggle “Mobile-Captured Fabric Dataset” (3,354 photos, 6 classes; licence unknown, research use only), our own labelled photos of tailor-shop scraps, and worker corrections.
  • Storage (plan): Postgres for ledger and passports; pgvector for image embeddings (a “similar scraps” memory) and document chunks.
  • Privacy: the camera captures fabric only, with no faces or personal data. The LLM receives only aggregated numbers.

sections.title: AI Layer
sections.html:
• Colour + purity: per-pixel colour naming and colour-family share. Grade A ≥ 85% purity, B ≥ 62%, C = mixed/print. Live now.
  • Fabric type: EfficientNet transfer learning, then TFLite on the phone. In progress; the prototype shows demo predictions.
  • Low confidence: scraps are flagged “check manually” instead of being auto-binned.
  • Correction loop: worker fixes become training data; retraining is weekly (Prefect) and the new model is used only if it is more accurate.
  • Retrieval (plan): nearest similar scraps from pgvector support uncertain predictions; “Ask Jhut AI” answers trader questions from buyer specs and EU rules (hybrid search + reranker + Bangla query rewriting).
  • Explainability: the scan shows the colour shares, the purity score and the top fabric probabilities behind each decision.

sections.title: Performance & Scalability
sections.html:
• Target per scan: about 1 second on a mid-range phone, offline.
  • Load (illustrative): a yard sorting 300 kg a day logs hundreds of bundles a day, which is light for one server.
  • Optimisation: vision runs on the device (no per-scan cloud cost); daily reports are generated in one overnight batch; a template is used on quiet days, so no LLM call is made.

sections.title: Security
sections.html:
• Now: static site, no personal data collected. This docs page uses client-side visibility and scheduling. That is suitable for a showcase, but it is not real access control.
  • Final build: login for traders and admins; role-based access (worker, supervisor, trader, admin); station tokens; signed Batch Passport links; encrypted storage.
  • Responsible AI: workers can override any decision, and every override is recorded in the passport.

sections.title: Analytics & KPIs
sections.html:
• Price uplift per kg sorted (target: up to 2.5× for white cotton grades)
  • Kilograms sorted per worker per day
  • Share of cotton sold to local recyclers instead of exported or downcycled
  • AI correction rate (falling over time means accuracy is improving)
  • Number of batches issued with a passport
